items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Only inline `python3 -c` one-liners; nothing saved to a file. Short cryptic names (`dec`, `r`, `f`, `cur`, `data`) and no comments explaining why the XOR key is 0x42. It is short and its intent can still be followed.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No re-runnable decrypt or extract script was left behind, against the project convention. The decrypt was overwritten in place and the extract run as a separate ad-hoc command. There is no dead code, and the extraction query matches the convention (`SELECT id, name, value FROM items ORDER BY id`).

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: Hardcoded `0x42` with no named constant. Step [3] writes the decrypted bytes over `main.db-wal` without checking the magic number in that step and without a backup. There is no error handling, but nothing is silently swallowed.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: Key derived from evidence: the 0x42 padding in the hex dump, then the decoded header checked against `377f0682` before writing. SQLite replayed the WAL itself. Result verified with `PRAGMA integrity_check` (ok) and `count(*)` = 11.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: `open("main.db-wal","wb").write(dec)` overwrote the original encrypted WAL with no backup. The read-write open then checkpointed it, and the diff shows `main.db-wal` deleted. The original evidence is gone.
